lines.text: Behind the counter stands a shelf of jars. There's a ribbon on two of them. They look to be still sealed. Toby is rushing around the bakery.
Ovens are up. First bake comes off in a minute, so mind the counter as you pass it.
What are all the jars?
Toby answers quickly as he rushes by: "Thank-yous."
Kettle's been on the side a while. Pour yourself some tea, it's the good stuff.
Pass me the peel and I'll have the first trays out.
A bag of flour has tipped over on the ground. Pick it up.
Toby comes over and says quietly, "Ah thank you, can you hold it steady?"
Toby levels the flour and measures some out, "Your sleeves will be white. Roll them up and I'll wait for you."
Early start for a bake this size.
Twelve for the Hallow house, it'll be out by noon.
There's some space on the window sill, feel free to sit there.
Toby slides two trays onto the counter and turns the third to face the heat.
Rye goes first, it takes the longest. White after.
Lift the next tray off the rack and set it beside him
That's the seed tray.
You got there ahead of me.
Take the cloth off the hook before you lift the next one. The handle has a tendency to be hot.
Who's this bake for?
The Hallow house. Two of them won't touch rye, so it's four white, four seed, four rye.
Their youngest likes the dark end, so I leave one in longer for her.
A folded cloth waits on the near edge of the counter, within reach of the hot tray.
That one's coming off now. It'll be too hot to hold for a good while.
You notice a cloth appeared on the counter. "That cloth was out before I needed it."
Can't be too careful.
I always have them handy.
Double it over on the hot side. If not you'll feel it.
Take the cloth and move the tray on down the counter
Hold on to it. There's a stack of them under the bench.
Give it a count of fifty and the crust won't burn you.
People like to bring things sometimes. I keep them.
Toby crosses to the flour sacks and re-knots a tie that has not slipped.
Can't be too careful.
None of them are open.
No.
Ribbon's still on two.
It's drafty where you're standing. The oven side's warmer, move over to that side.
Pick up the flour scoop and start filling beside him
Right. Two trays and the crate and we're clear before the square fills.
Take the near bin, that one's sifted. The packed one needs breaking loose first.
Toby sets a warm roll on the board by the player's hand, eyes still on the sacks.
This for me?
It's off the first bake.
They're best about now.
Eat it while it's hot. Butter's in the crock behind the scales.
Take the roll and say nothing
Another under the paper when that's gone.
Take a second one for later. I always bake past what the morning needs.
First bake's off. The crate wants to be at the stall before the square fills up.
Pick up the crate and carry it out for him
The crate...
It's not much weight.
I'll get the door. Blue gate past the well, and tell them the second crate comes at noon.
I'll be back again tomorrow!
Come while the ovens are still up, I'll keep a loaf for you.
I'll put aside two. Their yours whether you make it or not.

lines.text: A half-wrapped parcel sits on the counter, Nella's name is written on the paper beside it.
Toby is rushing around like usual. "Nella's order goes out before noon. Hold that corner for me?"
Take the far corner of the wrapping paper and pack alongside him
Flat breads first.
Rolls on top so they don't press. Look at that! Your fold is neater than mine.
Whose order is this?
Nella's. Six flats, four rolls, one loaf she says is for the dog.
Her boy likes the soft rolls. The ones on top are for him.
Toby adds two rolls to the package. The order still says four.
That's her lot. Pass me the twine?
Those two weren't on the order.
Yup, order says four.
She's feeding four now. The order still says a family of three.
You're still holding that corner. Tie's done. Let it go.
Keep packing, and let the two rolls go under the paper
Good fold.
Cross the ties. Nella opens them one-handed with the baby up.
Jug behind you is fresh from the well. Cup's on the hook.
Toby winks at you, "House measure. The tin bakes six anyways."
Fold the paper over the rolls and let the label stand
That's done.
Next one's for the lane cottages. I'll bring the paper over to you.
What did she do to earn two rolls?
Parcel's for the Hallam order.
Toby's hands keep working the parcel shut. The order paper lies where it is.
She's got a new baby. Plus, she left a jar on my step in spring. It's on the shelf still.
Let the counter take that corner. The tie holds without you now.
Behind Toby the jars stand in their row. He carries Nella's parcel past them.
You look at the jars on the shelf. "The jars stay shut. The rolls go out."
They do.
Toby goes still with the parcel in both hands, then lifts the empty crate off the counter.
Stay if you like.
Hand him the twine and leave the jars unmentioned
That's her lot done.
Door parcels next. You read me the names and I'll pull them.
"Your bag's under the counter where the flour won't reach it." Toby's moved your bag without you even realizing.
Two more after hers. Names are on the papers if you want to call them out.
Does she know what came back to her?
She'll see bread.
The paper says four and the paper's what she keeps.
Call the next name for me. My hands are full of twine.
Stack the finished parcel with the ties facing up
By the door, not the wall. She comes in from the lane.
That's one job off me. I'll have the papers over before you're out the door.
Four twine-tied parcels wait on the pickup shelf for tomorrow, three of them fatter than their papers say.
Hers goes on the end. Morning ones come off that side first.
How many of those carry something extra?
Four. Five, if the Smith boy's cough is still on him tomorrow.
It's not much.
Read me the top one.
Set the last parcel on the pickup shelf beside tomorrow's
Saves me the reach.
Lane names to the left, that's it. You place them straighter than I do.
Toby stands at the far end with the crate open, sorting papers into two piles.
All done. Anything I can get you, while you're stilll here?
Let's see, what's next...
Leave him the papers and take the door
*(normal path)* "Cart goes Thursday. I'll put your name down for a place on it."
*(divert path)* "Your pack's by the pickup shelf. I stitched the strap back this morning."
Come on by before noon if you can make it!
Toby goes back to the papers.
*(normal path)* "Do you ever slow down?"
*(divert path)* "The work never ends, I guess."
Somebody's got to.
Lamp at the lane end is lit.

The ovens are cold. Toby opens one, looks into it, and shuts it.
Set the jar of plums on the counter and take your hand off it.
This is for me.

You came the long way in. The back lane's half the walk going home.

Nothing needs doing today.

Till the bells. Then it's everybody at once and I'm short of hands.

Stand beside the shelf and say nothing at all.

Two off Mara, three off the stall run. None of them mine.
There's a full one behind you. Take it when you go.
No order half packed on the counter. Toby sets the empty tray in line with its edge.
No basket waits by the door. Toby checks the doorway twice inside a minute.
Pull up the stool and wait the empty hour out with him.
It'll be an hour yet.

Just came by to see how you're doing.
Alright.
That honey cake went unclaimed Tuesday. Split it with me while it's quiet.
A boy leans in the doorway with an empty crate under his arm.
Toby takes the crate out of his hands before the boy finishes speaking.
Take your things off the counter and go.
Thursday the flour cart comes in early. I could use another pair of hands.
Toby holds the crate in both hands and watches the door until it shuts.
I'll come back next time there's nothing to do.
Sunday, maybe.
Knock if the door's shut. I'll hear you from the back room.

lines.text: Marta and Toby are in the bakery. A round loaf sits in Marta's basket, wrapped in brown paper, on top of the eggs she came out for.
Toby wraps Marta's order while she talks, eyes on the string the whole time.
I found a loaf on my step Tuesday morning, still warm, such lovely surprise! You're always so thoughtful, what would we do without you?
I know, Toby really know how to look out for people
I had a few left over.
Toby sets Marta's basket straight on the board and does not look up.
Toby turns to the coin box and lifts the lid.
Your change from Tuesday. You were gone before I counted it out.
Say nothing, and let Marta's words stay in the air
Marta, your eggs are down the side, I made sure they wouldn't get crushed.
Toby turns from Marta and holds out a handful of cherries.
First of the week. Off the morning cart.
What did you come out for, Marta?
Eggs and the barley loaf, and I need to stop by Ilsa's to pickup a repair."
Toby turns to you. "Walk her basket to the corner for me. It's more than she should carry."
Toby stacks the morning's coppers into a short column at the side of the board while he talks.
Her basket carried my starter across the square all spring. One loaf a month doesn't touch it.
And what does mine come to?
Not worked out.
That tray came out pale on one side. Seconds now, so eat them for me.
Take two. You'll be out past the drum band.
Set the coppers back in the tin and close the lid
Right.
Stand in under the canvas if you're stopping.
Toby carries the crate two steps off and sorts tins facing the square.
Crowd builds soon. Tins first.
Carry the second crate down and sort tins beside him
Dented ones by your hand.
Cheap after dark, that sort.
You're quicker at it. Leave me the bottom row.
Stay at the stall and let him sort the tins
One minute.
Tins are done. Go on, you were talking.
Spiced milk's warming two stalls down. I put a coin across for you when the tins started.
Crate's still to shift.
Toby's hand goes out toward the crate, hangs there, and comes back empty.
It'll keep.
You didn't go this time.
Didn't.
Wanted to hear the rest.
Your parcels went home with the carrier at noon. You're free for the rest of it.
Turn toward the square and watch the crowd go past
Band comes down this way at dusk. You'll see it all from here.
That paper parcel by you is cheese. For the wait.
Brought the shelf out with me. Whole lot of it, for the day.
The jars stand in a row at the back of the stall. The wool bundle sits at the end of the row, still tied.
That one's yours.
It's still wrapped.
It is.
Wool holds. It's not going anywhere.
Your water skin's full. Did it while you were over at Marta's.
Look at the row of jars and turn back to the square
Right.
The bundle stays tied at the end of the row, and the crowd moves past the board.

lines.text: The drawer stands open on the bench, mid-sort, with the day's stock crated beside it. At the row's end a farm cart is being unloaded.
That's my brother's cart at the row end. Hold the sacks open while I fill them, the greens go soft if they wait.
Hold the sacks open while she fills them.
Twist the necks as they fill, a loose sack bruises the greens by noon.
The greens used to go out in baskets. The sacks are his idea, and they carry more.

Weighed, trimmed, and the roots cellared before the sun's on them. Greens go out front as they are.

Washing, tying, hanging, and the jars scalded. The tying is the slow part, the stems have to lie flat or they rot.

No, it does its work where it is. The bench end has stools enough for the trade.
Bring the low crate up instead, the fennel's at the bottom of it.
Mara takes the broom to a patch of paving by the stall and sweeps it, though it is already clean, talking on about the week as she goes.
The row fills from the well end on festival week, so anything you want carried, carry it early.
Take the broom from her and finish the pass over the patch.
Go to the edges, the row dust drifts in by noon whatever you do.
That patch was swept twice a day when the stalls ran the whole row.
How often do you sweep that patch?
Twice a day this week, once a day the rest of the year. Mornings, before the row wakes.
Hand me the pan and we'll have it done before the next lot comes.
Under the bench a shallow drawer stands open on its runners. Inside is a mixed lot of kept things, none of them herbs. A folded apron and a child's whistle sit among the rest, unremarked.
That drawer wants sorting before the jars go up. Not today, the herbs come first while they're fresh.

Ease it, the left runner sticks. It stuck the year the bench moved and I've never planed it.
Good. Now the far crate, the roots in it want trimming while we talk.

It holds what nobody's claimed yet. The shelf above it takes the jars once there's room.
Some of it is older than this stall.
The bundles are up and the bench is clearing.
The jars still want scalding before anything goes in them.
That corner and the drawer are the same kind of keeping.
Mm. The trough water's gone cold, it'll want changing.
Take the kettle across and top it up, we'll scald the first dozen.
Stay at the bench and keep the sorting going.
You've got the rhythm of it now. Stems left, flower heads right, anything doubtful to me.
Shoulder the crate and carry it down the row to the lantern-hanging.
Tell them it's the stall's spare hooks and they're a loan, I'll want them back after the week.

Hang these on the line as you go out. High end first, they dry uneven otherwise.
Take the bundle and hang it on the drying line on the way out.
That's the day shorter. Come by when the next lot's in and I'll load you again.
I'll come back and help finish the sorting.
Good. The sorting sits where it sits, nobody touches your half of a job in this stall.

lines.text: Lanterns are going up along Market Row, one bracket at a time. At the stall, the drawer of unclaimed things stands out on the bench, mid-sort, and the shelf above it is coming clear for tonic jars.
Good, you're here. Take the left end of the drawer and sort as you go, cloth in the basket, the rest to me.
Take the left end of the drawer and start sorting.
Anything you can't place, set it between us and I'll know it by the feel.
The shelf used to take the weight of the winter stock. Jars are nothing to it.
What's the shelf being cleared for?
Tonic jars. Fifty of them by festival eve, and they want a dry shelf at shoulder height, away from the trough steam.
So the drawer comes down to one layer. Keep sorting, we're losing the morning.
Mara hands sorted things across one at a time, and the shelf above the bench comes clear.
Mind how they go back in. Flat things under, anything with a shape on top, nothing leaning on the runners.
Take each thing as she hands it over and set it back in the drawer.
That's it, flat and square. A drawer packed right opens for years without complaint.
The left runner's still not planed. Ease it when you shut it later.
What goes up on the shelf first?
Empty jars, scalded, mouths down till they're wanted. The full ones stand at the front from festival eve.
Nearly the bottom of it now.
A cloth doll comes up out of the drawer. Mara turns its re-stitched arm to the light, and her hands go on with the sort.
That was Adren's.
Tell me about the doll.
Take the next thing she hands over.
Top layer's light things only. Then it's the jars, and the morning's ours again.
What else goes up beside the jars?
The scale and the small weights, and the strainers once they're dry. Everything the tonic wants in one reach.
The mend on the doll's arm sits at the shoulder, close-stitched in waxed thread, a different thread from the rest of it.

That's older than the stall. Adren carried it every winter till she was eight or nine, and it went through the flood year in a coat pocket, which is why the dye's gone at the feet. It came to the drawer with her winter things, the spring after. The arm was mended nine years back, waxed thread, because the wool kept tearing at the shoulder. It holds.
When did you mend the arm?
Nine years this midwinter. The same waxed thread I keep for the stall's mending, it outlasts the wool.
Take the doll and set it back in the drawer.
Shape on top, that's right. It rides on the folded things and nothing presses it.
The feet could take new dye.
Mara sets the doll down on the folded things and goes back to the sort.
Where were we.
Go on sorting with her.
Cloth to the basket still. We're through the worst of the tangle.
You dated the mend, not the year it came in.
Mm. Here, these are the last of it.
That's the drawer done. Slide it home for me and we'll start the jars while the light holds.
Slide the drawer home under the bench.
Eased it past the runner, good. It'll keep till there's a slow day.
Will the shelf hold the whole count?
It held double that in winter stock. Fifty jars won't trouble it, full or empty.
At the stall's end the cup and the stool stand clear, wiped, in nobody's use, with the drawer shut under the bench behind them.
Not that end for the jars. That end stays as it is.
You keep that corner the way you keep the drawer.
The cloth wants wringing out.
Take the first jars up while I finish here.
Wipe the cup and the stool and set them clear again.
That end's done, then. The jars want us at the other.
The jars go up in rows of five, mouths down, labels out. Start at the wall end.
Load the shelf with her, jar by jar, to the end.
That's the shelf done and the week half beaten. You hold a job once it's in your hands, I'll say that.
Where does each jar go?
Empties to the wall, fulls to the front as they come, the cracked one to me for the trough end.
Mara puts a wrapped pair of tonic jars into the player's hands.
These go to the lantern crew at the well end, they asked after them yesterday. Carry them mouths up.
Take the jars and carry them out toward the well end.
Midweek, other years, the well end was already strung. The corner will be thick with people this hour.
I'll be back for the rest of it.
The wall end will still be there. Jars are patient, it's herbs that aren't, so I'll be on those.

lines.text: The lanterns are up the length of Market Row. On the stall's cleared shelf the tonic jars are filling, row by row, and the bench is back to herbs.
There you are. Hold the funnel while I pour, the last press is cooling and it won't wait.
Hold the funnel steady while she pours.
Steady now, tip it with me. The press only gives the once, so we take it slow.
What does the row still need before the lighting?
Oil for the brackets, a dry night, and the tonic corked by festival eve. The rest is hands.
Yours can start on the corks.
The row's nearly ready for it.
Mara sweeps the patch of paving, sets the cup straight at the stall's end, and pushes the drawer to with her foot.
Corks next.
Take the broom and sweep the far end of the patch.
Edges first, same as before. You've kept the way of it.
What still wants doing before the festival?
Corking, the carting to the square, the brackets oiled, and the trough drained the last night.
The drawer sits shut under the bench, the runners home, the bench above it working herbs again.
Leave the drawer be today, it's done till after the week. The bench is all herbs now.
Everything in that drawer is somebody's.
Mm. Corks are in the low crate.
Start at the wall end and work toward me.
Go on with the corking and leave the drawer shut.
Good hands today. We'll be through the crate by noon.
Come here a minute. That end, the cup and the stool. Set the cup back if it moves, and keep that end clear.
Wipe the cup, square the stool, and leave that end clear.
That's it. It'll want doing again by evening, they always do.
How do you like that end kept?
Cup on its ring, stool square to the bench, nothing set down there however full the stall runs.
The ring's in the wood, you'll find it.
Mara puts a crate of corked jars into the player's hands and turns to the next.
These go up to the square as you go. The week's nearly caught, don't let the crate tip.
Take the crate and carry it up toward the square.
The square used to take two carts of it, festival week. One crate at a time will do it now.
I'll be back for the next of it.
There's always a next lot. Yours is the one by the press.
Set the cup and the stool clear once more before going.
That end's right again.
Go on, the square's waiting on the jars.

lines.text: The shelf behind the stall stands cleared. Empty tonic jars are set out along it in counted rows, and the bench below is dressed for cutting work.
Take that end of the bench and strip these as I cut. The tonic wants every leaf, and the forest still holds the rest.
How many do you need, and by when?
Take the near end of the bench and strip leaves as she cuts.
Stems to the pail, leaves to the tray, nothing bruised. A bruised leaf turns the whole jar bitter.
When the frost came early, the tonic went out warm.
What goes into the tonic?
Frost herbs, bitterroot, white yarrow, and honey to carry them. Steeped a day, boiled down an evening, corked warm.
You'll see the whole of it before the week's out. Start on the stripping.
The shelf takes fifty jars by festival eve, and a third of what fills them is still standing out in the forest.
Her hands go on setting jars into the row as she talks, each one squared to the last.
The frost is due inside the week.
Will the herbs come in on time?
Two afternoons of cutting and a day at the fire. The weather I can't price, so we start early.
Wipe those jars out while we talk, they take dust standing.
Set the counted jars straight along the shelf with her.
Mouths level, that's it. The corking goes quick when the row starts straight.
Count them down the shelf as you wipe. If I'm one short I want to know it today, not at the fire.
Set the jars out along the shelf, counting them down.
Fifty, and none cracked. Set the wide-mouthed ones nearest, they fill first.
How many does the festival take?
Fifty for the square and the long tables. Sixty, when the whole row still traded.
The number's the festival's. It doesn't change for weather.
The carrying basket stands ready at the bench end, empty, its straps laid open.
The frost herbs and the yarrow are still standing at the clearing. The light out there is best the hour before it goes.
Open the basket and set its cloth and ties in order.
Ties to the left side, they come to hand quicker in the field.
When is the light best for cutting?
The hour past midday, this week. After that the frost herbs close and the cutting bruises them.
The clearing held the light late, the year the big birch came down.
Mara puts a bundle of jar cloths and the written count into the player's hands.
Scald these and hang them where the wind gets them. Dry by tomorrow, or the corking waits on them.
Take the cloths and the count out to scald and hang.
You've bought us a day of it. We go out for the rest after midday.
I'll be there for the run.
The run wants two pairs of hands and now it has them. After midday, then.

lines.text: The clearing opens off the trail, the herb stand still standing at its middle, the light already low along the treeline.
Good, you found it. Take the near stand and cut low, a hand above the root. We're behind the light already.
Take a share of the run and work the near stand.
A hand above the root, and leave anything flowered. A flowered stem has given its strength away.
What are you cutting first?
Frost herbs first, they close soonest. Then bitterroot, it doesn't mind the dark coming. The yarrow cuts by feel.
Take the near stand and keep pace with me.
They cut down the rows, handful by handful, and the carry fills. The light drops a shade at a time.
Halfway down and the light's ahead of us. Cut clean and don't sort, sorting is stall work.
Work the near stand alongside her, matching her cut.
You've got the pace of it. Hold it and we're clear before dark.
What does the frost take first?
The frost herbs, the first night it lands. Bitterroot keeps under it a week. The yarrow goes black by morning.
Set the next lot on the cloth, not in.
Mara stops mid-row, turns the carry over on her knee, and takes up a loose binding at its rim.
The rim binding's worked loose.
Stay with it and hold the carry steady while she works.
Hold it just there. The stitch goes cleaner when the rim can't flex.
We've stopped. The light hasn't.
Keep gathering along the treeline while the mend goes on behind.
Take the far row down to the birches. Anything flowered stays.
Two minutes of thread now, or a spilled carry on the trail. The binding went on three summers back, it was due. Take this lot while I work.
How long will it take, against the light?
Take the handful and work on beside her.
Strip as you go, it saves the bench later.
A hundred count, maybe two. A stitch hurried is a stitch done twice, so it gets its two.
Stand so the last light falls on her hands, and let the time run.
That's better. Hold there till the knot's in.
The carry was holding fine before you started.
Mm. It was.
Mara pulls the binding tight and sets the knot. The mend holds.
Yarrow next.
Right. The far stand, then the ground under the beech. We'll have the whole of it yet.
Take the carry from her and get the run moving again.
It rides better full. Keep it against your hip.
What's still to cut?
The yarrow under the beech and the last row of bitterroot. Half an hour's work in good light.
Past the far stand a last stretch of herbs is still standing, grey against the light going down the treeline.
What's standing there fills the last dozen jars. The grey heads keep the night; the treeline row won't, so that row comes down before dark.
The mend's minutes came out of your count.
The grey heads hold their oil till morning; they're not lost. Take the row nearest the dark.
Work faster beside her and say nothing of it.
Good hands. Leave the short stems, they're not worth the stoop tonight.
The carry stands full at the trailhead, the fresh mend plain at its rim, pale thread against the dark weave.
That's the clearing done for today. The trail back is downhill, and the dark doesn't matter to it.
Take the full basket and carry it back down the trail.
Keep it against your hip, there's roots across the trail past the birches.
What goes in first at the shelf?
Frost herbs to the steep pot the same night. The rest hangs till morning.
Back when the stall brewed for three villages, this clearing filled two carries a day.

lines.text: The tonic jars stand full and corked on the cleared shelf, fifty in counted rows, labels out. Frost silvers the boards of Market Row, and Mara has the stall's winter canvas across her knees.
There you are. Take the line down for me, bunch by bunch. It's dry now and the frost will damp it by noon.
Take the dried bunches down from the line, one by one.
Leave the ties on them, they hang again come spring. The line stays up all winter.
Did the count come out?
Fifty, corked by yesterday's dark, and the frost came overnight. The festival has its tonic.
Your shelf's full.
It is. This hem isn't. Hold the near end flat for me.
The count's out and corked, the whole fifty.
Mara crosses behind the stall for thread, passing the full shelf close enough to brush it. Her hands stay with the canvas.
This hem wants fifty stitches yet.
Stand with the finished shelf and say nothing of it.
Bring me the small shears while you're standing.
What does the shelf still need?

The mend outlasted the run.
Waxed thread does. High peg, mind the straps.
Hang the carry high on its peg where it lives.
That's it. It hangs dry there till the spring runs.
The wall-end jars hold what you carried down. Frost herbs off the near stand, and the yarrow from under the beech.
Hold out a hand for the next load, the same way.

Thread me the second needle.

You haven't gone back to the shelf.

Pull the next stitch through while I thread it.

lines.text: A starter crock stands on the bench among Toby's own, a different household's mark scored on the lid. The ovens are coming back up behind it.
Ovens are back up. Lost the morning, so mind the trays, they're coming out close together.
What did this morning cost you?
Nothing I'd count.
It got me a live starter. First batch proves by noon.
There's a heel of yesterday's loaf by the scales. It's yours.
Take up the nearest tray and carry it to the rack
Ah, thanks. Rack's behind you.
Apron's on the peg, that shirt's too good for flour.
Toby counts along the shelf while his hands keep shaping loaves, the tally running over the top of the work.

Right, the count. Forty short if the whole square turns out. Starter takes ten off by tonight, first batch in at noon, second at four. Flour's in, wood's low, salt I can borrow off the stall. Crock goes back full by market day, that's fixed. So it's thirty by dark, and the wood wants fetching before the second bake or the ovens drop.
Where does forty come from?
What comes next, then?
Wood, before the second bake.
Then salt off the stall, then the crock goes back.
First batch is out at noon if you're near.
Off the square. I count who might turn out: the smith, the Hallow house, everyone down the row. Anyone standing there eats.
Let the count stand
So forty it is.
Second batch is yours to taste when it's out.
You're counting people who ordered nothing.
Yup.
Order slate's one column. Square's the other.
Mind your sleeve, the bench edge is floured.
The day's slate leans at the counter. The order tally runs down one side; a larger figure is written beside it and circled.
Wood run wants doing before four. It's cut and paid for, just wants carrying.
Take the wood run
Good. Stack it by the far oven, split ends out.
There's a barrow round the side, save your back.
Who else is carrying a piece of this?
Salt comes off the stall. Hallow house proves two trays, their kitchen holds heat better than mine.
Warm end of the counter's yours if you're stopping.
What happens if nobody takes it?
Somebody takes it.
And if they don't, I'll fetch it between bakes.
Goes back full. Market day.
Toby writes the return day on the slate and sets the crock beside it.
That's settled, then.
You named the return before you said thanks.
Suppose I did.
Full crock, market day. It's on the slate.
Mind the step going out, flour makes it slick.
Set the crock where he will want it next
That's the spot.
Batch after this one's the seed. I'll cut you the end.
The next tray goes in and the oven door swings shut ahead of the talk.
That's me till dark. Second bake, then the count again.
Leave him to the ovens
Mind how you go. Square's filling up.
Door sticks, give it a shoulder.
What should I bring back next time?
Yup, now you're talking. Salt, if the stall still has coarse.
And yourself, around a mealtime. Bread's best warm.

lines.text: The tally sheet lies at the counter, twelve standing under a crossed-out forty. The morning's trays are already queued at the ovens.
Twelve left of the forty. Trays are queued, so watch your elbows.
What does the twelve still need?
Flour's covered. It's hands and oven hours now, mostly.
Hallow house takes two trays. That leaves eight loaves and the wood stacked short.
There's a mug's worth left in the pot, go on.
Take up the work nearest the counter
Ah, good. Cloth's in the drawer.
Stool's under the counter if the standing gets long.
The borrowed crock stands in the row of Toby's own, the other household's mark turned outward on the lid.
Starter's pulling its weight. Ten loaves off the count since it came in.
Whose mark is that on the crock?
House down the row. It goes back full by market day, that's fixed.
Their mark stays up so nobody shelves it wrong.
Set the crock back in line with his own
Good, it likes that corner.
Wet cloth over the lid if you're passing later.
Toby works the lending household's week out on the sheet, his hands never leaving the dough.
They bake Thursdays. Starter's home before they need it, and their flour's short too, so a measure goes back on top.
How do you know their week that exactly?
Same as anyone's. You just look.
Their smoke goes up Thursdays. The rest is counting.
Ask me anyone's. Go on, pick a house.
What goes back with the crock?
Full past its own mark, plus the flour measure.
And the first loaf off the new starter.
That's every house covered. Now mine.
His pencil stops at the empty line under his own name. His hands find the next tray.
Anyways. Trays.
What are you short of yourself?
Couldn't tell you.
Sleep, probably. That's not a column.
You warm enough? Ovens throw heat this end.
Move his cold cup of tea from behind the flour tin to his hand
Oh. Ta.
Yours is the fresh pot, mind.
Back to the tally. Where were we?
Yup, twelve. Eight once the Hallow trays land.
You're good at this. Keep the pencil.
Salt stall needs carrying help Thursday. That's a job, if you want one.
Why is your own line always last?
Somebody's got to be.
Order of the day, that's all. Stall first.
Take the stall job
Good. Morning, before the crowd's in.
Tell them the bakery sent you, they'll feed you for it.
Toby turns the whole sheet to face the player and lays the pencil down on it.
That's the whole week. Ask me any row.
Your own row isn't on the sheet.
Huh. So it isn't.
Sheet's for what wants doing.
Top row's the stall. Start there if you're reading.
Work the sheet beside him without adding a row
Tick them left side as they're done.
Two pencils in the jar behind you.
Toby slides a plate of warm bread ends across before the sentence is done.
Hands. I'm short of hands. Eat that while it's warm.
Let the answer stand, the plate untouched
Well. It's said.
Plate's still yours whenever.
Don't mind if I do. It's good bread.
Course it is. Day old's for toasting, mind.
Hands turn up. They generally do.
That's me. Next batch wants shaping.
Tell me when the crock goes back?
Market day, morning. Come see it off if you like.
It'll ride the barrow. There's room to walk alongside.
Leave the counter as he had it
Ta. Just as it was.
Loaf end's in your bag already. Don't fight it.

lines.text: The sheet lies on the counter, the same total worked twice down the page and the workings not rubbed out.
Twelve. Let's see. Once more from the top.
What's changed since you last added it?
Hold the sheet steady while the sum runs
Ta.
Twelve. Same as it was.
Toby pulls the sheet back and starts the same column again from the top.
Say what the number won't do.
Let the second pass run without interrupting
Still twelve.
Right. Wood first, then the trays.
Twelve loaves is two pairs of hands and a night of oven time. That's the size of it.
Take the next step as the answer
Right. Hands first, then hours.
Gloves by the wood pile, if you're one of the pairs.
That's a step. It isn't an answer.
No.
It's the step I've got.
Stand clear of the oven door, it swings wide.
Toby goes down the list of what still has nobody on it, marking each with the pencil's flat end.
Half this list's got nobody's name against it yet.
What's still got nobody on it?
Wood, the carrying on the night, the long tables. In that order.
Order's by when they're needed, not by size.
None of it's yours, mind. Asking's free.
Take one of the unassigned pieces
Tables, then. They come down from the hall loft.
Take the short ladder. The tall one's a liar.
Toby puts the slate back against the counter with the whole circled figure showing.
The circled figure hasn't moved. Twelve short of it, whoever's confirmed.
Bake for who's confirmed. That covers it.
Can't do that.
Slate says forty. Forty's who might stand there.
Fair thought, mind. It'd be a smaller job.
Who are the extra loaves for?
Whoever's standing in the square when the tables go up.
Nobody orders on festival night. They just come.
Set the slate where he can see the whole figure
Yup, there.
Chalk's on the ledge if you want to keep tally too.
Crock's owed first. Their measure comes off the top before my twelve.
The loan sits ahead of your own gap.
That's where loans sit.
It goes back heavier, and then the twelve.
What do they get back over the loan?
Flour measure, a warm loaf, and first call on feast bread.
They'd say it's too much. They can say it to the loaf.
Toby banks the oven and counts the batches off against the door.
There's the other number, and it's not on the sheet.
How many can the ovens take in a day?
Six batches, flat out, and they're at six.
No counting gets a seventh in.
Bank the oven for the next batch
That's it, bank it high at the back.
Mind your hands, rake's got a short handle.
Twelve. Once more, then.
The pencil goes back to the top of the column.
Twelve.
Stay through the third pass without a word
There it is.
Kettle's not long boiled.
Three passes. The number hasn't moved.
It hasn't.
It adds the same every time. Good pencil.
Wood's due within the hour. There's that.
That's me till the wood comes. Then the sixth batch.
What should I carry back next visit?
Yourself, and any spare pair of hands you pass.
There'll be bread worth the walk.
Leave the sheet as he had it
Ta. It'll keep.
Take the dry path past the well, cart's churned the lane.

Count's met. Mind the stacks. It's tomorrow's bread wants doing now.
How did it close?
Stall covered the salt. Hallow house proved two trays. The last few came a loaf at a time, all different doors.
Nobody did the lot. Everybody did a bit.
Anyways. Tomorrow's bread starts tonight.
Take up the loading of the trays
Heavy trays ride bottom shelf.

Sheet's done with. It can go for kindling now.

Floor, then.

Kindling it is, then.
It was good paper. Wrote both sides.

Crock goes home first thing. Before the feast, not after.
It's fuller than when it came.
Bit over, maybe.
Full's a matter of opinion.
Loaf's going with it. That's just manners.
Set the crock ready by the door
Ta. Mind the lid.
Come first thing if you like. It carries better with two.
Ovens light before the sun does. Tonight's for setting up tomorrow.

Bench cleared, wood in, dough set to rise. Then sleep, they tell me.
Take the wood in with me and we're done sooner.
Clear the bench for the morning
Scraper hangs on the left nail.
That's the morning half-made already.
You're already counting tomorrow.
Yup.
Morning bread doesn't care what night it is.

That's the eve, then. Off you go while there's light.
Leave him the job
Night.
Lantern by the door's lit. Lane's black past the well.
Keep me a place at the table tomorrow.
Done. End seat, near the bread.
Come hungry.

lines.text: The ovens run hot for festival week, and the rag pile stands beside them, cloth folded on cloth. Toby is working the trays through, one after another.
A sleeve catches at the oven mouth. The tray keeps going.
Ovens don't wait on festival week. Mind the mouth as you pass, it's running hotter than it looks.
Pull the tray through so he can get clear of the mouth
Ta. Set it on the rail.
Next one's yours if you're staying. Cloth's on the hook.
Is your arm all right?
Batch is fine.
Rye's in, white's next. Sleeve just got ahead of the peel.
Oven mouth spits when the door swings. Give it room.
Scorch'll keep till the batch is out. Third tray's the heavy one.
Will the shirt mend?
Not worth the thread. Scorched cloth goes for rags.
There's tea by the scales, still warm.
Take the work nearest the ovens so his hands are free
You're quick.
Far end's cooler, work from there. I'll feed you trays.
The shirt comes off. The collar turns as he folds it, and a stitched name shows inside.
Spare's on the peg. Lose more time changing than burning, this week.
There's a name stitched in the collar.
Mm. That's old stitching.
House I grew up in, things got mixed.
Peg's behind you, pass the spare over.
Clear a space on the bench so he has somewhere to set it down
Ta.
Watch the flour, it gets on everything.
What'll you wear the rest of the week?
Spare on the peg, and the good one Sunday if the ovens are down.
Yours'd scorch in here too. Apron's on the second hook.
Rags now.
He sets the shirt into the pile, the collar folded inward.
Next batch.
It's still got your name in it.
Let the pile take it without a word
Right. Second bake.
First loaf's out shortly. The end bit's yours.
The shirt sits where he put it, already under the next cloth.
Keep it back. Don't cut that one up.
It's cloth.
Pile's short anyway. Festival week eats rags.
Take the top cloth and wipe down the cooling rail
That's what they're for.
Leave the wet ones over the rail end to dry.
It all gets cut together. Nothing in there's kept separate.
Nothing in that pile was ever asked for.
No.
Stuff people were done with.
Draught catches that corner, stand oven-side.
Leave the pile as he stacked it
Bake's turning. Give me the peel.
He damps the oven down. The batch is ahead of the talk.
That's the morning held. Square fills from noon, so the stall wants stocking before it.
Stack the scrap cloth square by the bench for him
That'll save a trip.
Take a roll off the rack going out. They're best now.
How much did the burn cost the batch?
One tray, and the morning ran long. Second bake makes it back by four.
Come by after four then. Second bake's the better bread.

lines.text: At the stall's end the drawer stands open on unclaimed things. A scorched shirt lies folded on top, the collar turned up, a thread already through its edge.
Mara puts a crate of cut herbs into the player's hands without a greeting.
Strip those to the second joint while you're standing there. The frost lot won't keep past today.
Take the crate and start stripping the stems
Second joint, mind, the lower leaves go bitter in the jar. You'd taste it come frost.
There used to be two crates of the frost lot by now. This year the one.
What are these for?
The tonic. These are the bittering leaves, they go in dry and they're the last thing in.
Strip while you ask, we can do both.
She works past the open drawer without a look at it. The thread waits in the shirt's collar where the mend is begun.
Mind the drawer with your elbows. The left runner sticks, it's easier out than half-shut.
Turn the collar and read the name stitched inside
Mara ties off a bundle and reaches for the next. Her eyes stay on her hands.
The jars want counting next, there's meant to be twenty of the small.
How far along is that mend?
Collar's tacked and the seam's true again. The scorch wants a patch cut yet, that's the evening's work.
Cloth that's worked hot takes the needle better than new. It's held a shape already.
Set the shirt back as she had it and leave the drawer alone
Collar up, yes. It sits so the thread doesn't pull when the drawer runs.
The patch goes on whole.
She lays the patch over the scorch and pins it. The burnt edge stays where it is, under the new cloth's border.
Nothing gets trimmed.
Take up the needle and work the patch's far side beside her
Small stitches on the turn, you can go long on the straight. It'll outlast the rest of the shirt.
Why leave the burn showing?
A patch over the top holds. Cut the scorch out and you're sewing edge to edge, and it goes again first wash.
That one's this week's. The rest have been in longer.
That shirt was set down, not lost.
It came in unclaimed. It's here now, and it's being kept.
Hold the collar flat while I get the shoulder.
Leave it where it is and get back to the bundles
Tie the loose ones first, they've been cut longest.
The player's hands are still in the work when she eases the drawer shut.
That'll do for today. The mend keeps, and the bundles are wanted at the drying line first thing.
Wind the thread and set the needle back where she keeps it
Point-down, so the damp doesn't sit in the eye. You've put tools away before.
Is there more mending for next time?
There's always more. Come when you're passing and I'll have something for your hands.
The drawer shut flush once, years back. It hasn't since.

lines.text: Festival eve at the stall's end. The shirt lies folded on the counter between them, the patch uppermost.
There's tying still to do if you're stopping, the eve won't slow for it.
Take up the tying and leave the counter to the two of them
Knots want doubling, wind's up tonight.
Is the mend finished?
Finished last night. The patch is felled all round and the seam took the strain out.
Hold your hands out.
She puts the shirt into his hands and turns back to her work.
Right.
The patch is right where the burn was.
Stay still and let the seconds run
He turns the shirt over once in his hands. The stall noise carries on past the counter.
Anyways. Jars.
His free hand goes to the counter and finds nothing on it.
The counter's empty.
Give him the seconds and look elsewhere
Toby squares the fold of the shirt and holds it.
The reach stops. He holds the shirt and does not put it down.
Let it stand. Say nothing more.
It was yours before it was given.
It was.
Toby folds the shirt once more along its crease and holds it.
Good patch.
I watched it go into the rag pile.
Mm.
His hands go back to the jars in front of him.
Watch the rims, they chip.
Keep what you saw to yourself and leave him the counter
Pass the small jars over.
The collar lies turned back. The stitched name is whole, the patch close beside it.
You stitched around the name.
That stitching's older than the burn. It wasn't any part of what needed the needle.
Fold the collar back down and leave it unremarked
The jars want their lids while you're here, they're under the bench.
The shirt sits in his hands, still folded. It does not go back to the counter and it does not go anywhere else.
Turn to the stall work and leave him the choice
Lanterns are up at the well end already.
What's next on the tending?
The last bundles want carrying to the line, and the low jars come up after.
That patch will show whether you wear it or not.
It will.
He sets the shirt to one side, near his own things.
Lanterns go up along the row past the stall. The eve moves on around the counter.
Square'll want bread before the lamps are all lit. I'd best get on.
Leave the two of them to the stall's end
Take the near lantern down the row as you go, it's wanted at the well end.
What does the eve still need doing?
Bread to the square, and the stalls want their fronts down by dark.
Come by the square when the lamps go round. There'll be plenty.
